name: Baking soda deodorant

angle.text: Users apply sodium bicarbonate deodorants, store-bought or home-made, to keep underarm odour down and present as clean. It is among the oldest patented deodorant ingredients; trials of this specific use are lacking.

summary: A DIY and natural-deodorant staple made with sodium bicarbonate; long used, but untested in trials.
note: No clinical trials; alkaline, with anecdotal reports of underarm irritation.
currentQuick:
Baking soda deodorant uses sodium bicarbonate, alone or mixed with other ingredients, to manage underarm odour. It is one of the earliest patented deodorant ingredients and a common home recipe.
No published trials were found for it as a deodorant.
How it works: It acts on odour, not sweat. It is mildly alkaline and is said to neutralise odour, though its general odour-absorbing effect has little evidence behind it.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources list eye irritation as its main hazard. Anecdotal reports of underarm irritation exist, but no published study of this was found.
deepLead:
Baking soda deodorant refers to deodorants made with sodium bicarbonate, either commercial products or home-made mixtures applied to the underarms. Wikipedia lists sodium bicarbonate among the earliest patented deodorant ingredients and notes it appears in some dry and wet deodorants, alone or combined with other ingredients.
Sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline in solution, and has long been promoted as an odour absorber, although the Wikipedia article on the compound says there is little evidence that it absorbs odours in general. Patent literature includes a 2004 deodorant towelette system soaked in a solution that includes baking soda.
No clinical studies of baking soda deodorants were found.

name: Apple cider vinegar for odour

angle.text: Folk-remedy followers wipe diluted vinegar on the underarms in the belief that its acidity curbs odour. The idea rests on anecdote and has not been tested for this purpose.

summary: A home remedy of wiping vinegar on skin to curb odour; untested for this use, with burn warnings.
currentQuick:
Some people wipe apple cider vinegar on the underarms or body to reduce odour. It is a folk remedy tied to natural-grooming culture.
No published study has tested it for odour, and reference sources report poor evidence for its health claims generally.
How it works: People say the acetic acid lowers skin pH and makes the skin less hospitable to odour-causing bacteria, which break down apocrine sweat.
Risks and caveats: Reference sources say applying it to skin may cause burns. Acid content varies between commercial brands.
deepLead:
Applying apple cider vinegar to the skin, typically the underarms, to reduce body odour is a folk remedy. Apple cider vinegar is about 5% acetic acid in water, made by fermenting apple cider, and is promoted for many health purposes.
Body odour arises mainly when skin bacteria break down secretions from apocrine sweat glands. Believers say the acidity of vinegar suppresses these bacteria; no published trials were found testing apple cider vinegar for this purpose.
Wikipedia reports that evidence for apple cider vinegar's health claims in general is poor and that applying it to skin may cause burns.

name: Chlorophyll internal deodorant

chain: Believed to neutralise odour from within
angle.text: Supplement users take chlorophyll or chlorophyllin as an internal deodorant for body, breath and waste odour. Human evidence for body odour specifically is essentially absent, so the appearance link rests on belief and anecdote.

summary: Oral chlorophyll or chlorophyllin pitched as an internal deodorant; the cited human evidence for body odor is essentially absent.
note: No controlled human trials for body odor found in cited sources.
currentQuick:
Chlorophyll and chlorophyllin are green plant-pigment products sold as oral 'internal deodorants' for body, breath and waste odor. The idea dates to the 1940s and returned via social media in the 2020s.
The cited reference material lists no controlled human trials of the odor claim.
How it works: Proponents say it neutralizes odor-causing compounds from within. Laboratory research has shown chlorophyllin binding some mutagens, but this has not been shown to apply to body odor.
Risks and caveats: The cited sources contain no safety discussion. It is sold as a supplement and used as a food colorant (E140/E141).
deepLead:
Chlorophyll internal deodorant refers to the oral use of chlorophyll or its water-soluble semi-synthetic derivatives, chlorophyllins, to reduce body, breath or waste odor. Chlorophyllins are salts made from chlorophyll, and the main food-additive forms are sodium chlorophyllins, listed as E140(ii) and E141(ii).
Oral preparations have been marketed for odor from incontinence, colostomies and body odor generally. The Wikipedia article on the topic flags this claim as lacking medical citation and cites no controlled human trials of body, ostomy or fecal odor. Laboratory and animal research on chlorophyllin has mostly concerned binding of mutagens rather than odor.

name: Zinc for body odor

chain: Claimed change in sweat or bacteria
angle.text: Supplement and appearance communities circulate the idea that taking zinc orally cuts body odour. Zinc is studied for deficiency, and the sources consulted give no trial support for this odour use.

summary: Oral zinc is sometimes claimed to cut body odor; the sources consulted give no support for this use.
note: Thin evidence; zinc is established only for deficiency.
currentQuick:
Zinc is an essential mineral sold as an over-the-counter supplement. Some online discussion links it to reduced body odor.
The sources consulted do not mention zinc in connection with body odor.
How it works: Proponents' mechanism is not documented in the sources consulted. Body odor is generally attributed to bacteria acting on sweat.
Risks and caveats: Not assessed in the sources consulted for this use. Oral zinc is used for deficiency repletion.
deepLead:
Zinc for body odor refers to the claim, circulated in supplement and appearance communities, that taking zinc orally reduces body odor. Zinc is an essential mineral; oral forms such as zinc gluconate and zinc acetate are used to treat or prevent zinc deficiency.
The reference pages consulted for this entry describe body odor as arising mainly from bacterial breakdown of sweat gland secretions and do not mention zinc as a factor or treatment.

name: Probiotics for body odor

angle.text: Some users take probiotics on the theory that the gut microbiome shapes how a person smells. Research links gut bacteria to systemic malodour, but human trials of probiotics for body odour were not found.

summary: Probiotics are floated for body odor via the gut-skin link; no human trials were found.
note: Gut-microbiome link is a research observation, not a tested treatment.
currentQuick:
Some people propose probiotics to change body odor through the gut microbiome. A 2020 study explored skin bacteria in the gut microbiome as markers of systemic malodor.
No trials of probiotics for body odor were found in the sources consulted.
How it works: The proposed route is the gut microbiome influencing what is excreted through skin. This is not shown by trials in the sources consulted.
Risks and caveats: Not assessed in the sources consulted.
deepLead:
Probiotics for body odor is the idea that taking probiotic microbes, or altering the gut microbiome, changes how a person smells. Reference sources note that the gut microbiome can affect body odor, citing a 2020 study on cutaneous bacteria in the gut microbiome as biomarkers of systemic malodor.
Grokipedia mentions lactobacilli only as a topical skin treatment that may rebalance skin microbiota, and its citation for that statement appears mismatched, so it is not treated here as evidence.

name: Fruit and veg smell diet

angle.text: Users eat more fruit and vegetables hoping to make their natural scent more pleasant. A study of men associated higher intake with sweat rated floral, fruity and sweet, with the effect described as mild.

summary: Eating more fruit and vegetables is associated with more pleasant-smelling sweat in a study of men; effects are described as mild.
note: Association from a small body of work.
currentQuick:
Some people eat more fruit and vegetables hoping to smell better. A study of men found higher intake associated with sweat rated as more pleasant.
Sources describe the scents as mild.
How it works: Dietary compounds appear in sweat and may alter its perceived scent; the specific mechanism is not detailed in the sources consulted.
Risks and caveats: No risks documented in the sources consulted.
deepLead:
The fruit and veg smell diet is the practice of eating more fruit and vegetables in the belief that it makes sweat smell more pleasant. Wikipedia reports a study of males in which higher fruit and vegetable intake was associated with more pleasant-smelling sweat, described as floral, fruity, sweet and medicinal in quality.
Grokipedia likewise says these foods have been associated with more pleasant body odors, but notes the scents are not typically strong.

name: Cutting red meat for smell

angle.text: Users cut red meat in the belief that it makes their body odour more attractive to others. A controlled two-week study in men reportedly rated sweat from the meat diet as less pleasant and more intense; the evidence base is small.

summary: A controlled study in men reportedly rated sweat from a meat diet as less pleasant; evidence is small.
note: Based on one reported small controlled study.
currentQuick:
Some people cut red meat hoping to smell better. A controlled study of men on meat or non-meat diets reportedly found the meat group's odor rated less pleasant and more intense.
The evidence summarized here rests mainly on that one study.
How it works: Diet is thought to change compounds excreted in sweat; specifics are not given in the sources consulted.
Risks and caveats: Nutritional effects of dietary changes were not covered in the sources consulted.
deepLead:
Cutting red meat for smell is the practice of reducing red meat intake in the belief that it improves body odor. Grokipedia states that red meat intake has been shown to alter axillary odor, making it less attractive to others, and describes a controlled study in which male participants ate meat or non-meat diets for two weeks, with samples from the meat group rated less pleasant and more intense.
The study is cited by Grokipedia as 'Effect of Meat Consumption on Body Odor Attractiveness' in Chemical Senses; the page gives no authors or year. Wikipedia's body odor article does not discuss red meat.

name: Cutting garlic and onion

chain: Fewer sulfur compounds in breath and skin
angle.text: Users skip garlic and onion to avoid lingering breath and skin odour. Sulfur compounds such as allyl methyl sulfide are documented in breath and can persist for up to two days; direct trials on body odour are limited.

summary: Garlic compounds are documented in breath and skin emissions; avoiding garlic and onion is a plausible odor lever, with limited direct trials.
note: Odor compounds persist up to about two days.
currentQuick:
Garlic and onion contain sulfur compounds that appear in breath and skin emissions for up to two days. Some people avoid them to reduce odor.
Research measures the compounds and some countermeasures but not avoidance for social outcomes.
How it works: Allicin breaks down into allyl methyl sulfide, absorbed into the blood and released via lungs, kidneys and skin.
Risks and caveats: No risks documented in the sources consulted.
deepLead:
Cutting garlic and onion is the practice of avoiding these foods to reduce body and breath odor. Garlic breath arises mainly from volatile sulfur compounds, especially allyl methyl sulfide (AMS), formed as allicin breaks down; AMS is the longest-lasting and can persist for up to two days.
AMS is absorbed into the bloodstream and leaves the body through the lungs, kidneys and skin, which is why mouthwash and mints are described as not particularly effective. Grokipedia says garlic and onion produce AMS that is exhaled and secreted in sweat.

name: Cutting alcohol for smell

angle.text: People in appearance and grooming circles cut alcohol in the belief that sweat, breath and body odour become less noticeable. The idea rests on anecdote, with no dedicated studies behind it.

summary: Dropping alcohol to smell better: a common anecdote with no dedicated studies behind it.
note: Based on personal reports; no studies of alcohol abstinence and body odour were found.
currentQuick:
Some people stop or reduce drinking in the hope that their sweat and breath smell less. It is usually one step among several grooming changes.
General references list drink among the many factors affecting body odour, but no study found here tests abstinence for this purpose.
How it works: Body odour mainly arises when skin bacteria break down gland secretions; diet, drink, gut microbiome and genetics are listed as influences. Believers suggest alcohol adds to this.
Risks and caveats: Cutting alcohol is not itself associated with a documented odour-related harm in the sources reviewed. People who drink heavily are generally advised by clinicians to seek medical guidance before stopping suddenly.
deepLead:
Cutting alcohol for smell is a lifestyle practice in which people reduce or stop drinking alcohol in the belief that it will make their sweat, breath or general body odour less noticeable. It is discussed in appearance and grooming circles as part of a wider approach to smelling clean.
Body odour is generally attributed to bacterial activity on skin gland secretions, and encyclopedic sources list food, drink, gut microbiome and genetics among the influences on it. No published trial found in the sources reviewed here has tested alcohol abstinence specifically as a way to change body odour, so the practice rests largely on personal reports.

name: Carnivore diet smell

angle.text: Carnivore dieters report changes in body odour, with some describing a milder scent and others a stronger or fishy one. The reports are anecdotal and no one has measured the effect.

summary: Claims that eating only meat changes how you smell; reports go both ways and no one has measured it.
note: Anecdotal; the diet itself is criticised by dietitians' bodies.
currentQuick:
Followers of all-meat diets often say their body odour changes, sometimes for the better and sometimes not.
No study found here has measured odour on such a diet.
How it works: Skin bacteria break down gland secretions, and diet is one listed influence. Meat is high in carnitine and choline, which gut bacteria can convert to compounds with a fishy smell in susceptible people.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia says dietitian bodies list the carnivore diet among fad diets, citing risks such as lacking fibre, raised LDL cholesterol and nutrient gaps.[2]
deepLead:
Carnivore diet smell refers to claims about how an all-animal-product diet affects body odour, breath and sweat. Some adherents say their odour becomes milder, while others report the opposite.
The carnivore diet is a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet limited to meat, dairy and eggs; Wikipedia says nutrition bodies list it among fad diets and that it has no supporting clinical evidence. That article does not discuss body odour, and no study found here has measured odour on the diet.

name: Fish odor syndrome choline restriction

angle.text: People with trimethylaminuria, a rare condition that gives sweat and breath a fishy smell, discuss choline restriction as one dietary approach. It is used in medically supervised management of the condition rather than as a general grooming tactic.

summary: A diet approach to a rare genetic condition that makes sweat and breath smell fishy; managed by medical supervision.
note: Choline is essential; restriction is cautioned against in pregnancy and complete elimination is not advised.
currentQuick:
Trimethylaminuria is a rare condition in which a fishy-smelling compound builds up and appears in sweat, urine and breath. Some people also use the term loosely for unexplained smell worries.
Choline restriction is one of the dietary strategies described for it.
How it works: A deficient FMO3 enzyme fails to convert trimethylamine to an odourless form; diets high in choline or carnitine supply more raw material.
Risks and caveats: Choline is an essential nutrient, so Wikipedia says complete elimination is not advised and restriction is cautioned against in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Management is described as best done under medical or nutritional supervision.[1]
deepLead:
Trimethylaminuria (TMAU), also called fish odor syndrome, is a rare metabolic condition in which the body cannot adequately convert trimethylamine, a compound that smells like rotting fish, into odourless trimethylamine N-oxide. Choline restriction is one dietary approach discussed for managing it.
Most cases are inherited through mutations in the FMO3 gene. Wikipedia says there is no known permanent cure and that symptoms are usually managed through diet under medical or nutritional supervision.

name: Washing clothes properly

chain: Odour and residue removed from fabric
Clothes smell fresh on the body
angle.text: Users launder clothes carefully so garments do not hold odour, dirt or stains, which keeps their overall presentation clean. Fresh-smelling, well-kept fabric is an immediately noticeable part of grooming.

summary: Basic laundry technique, raised in looksmaxxing mainly to stop clothes holding smell.
note: General laundry references do not address odour directly.
currentQuick:
This covers ordinary laundry practice: detergent, agitation, rinsing and drying. People interested in smelling clean often examine it.
The general reference used here does not address odour specifically.
How it works: Detergent surfactants lift dirt, agitation loosens it and rinsing removes it; temperature affects chemical activity and fabric shrinkage.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes heat and agitation can shrink wool and hot water can cause colour loss, so care labels matter.[1]
deepLead:
Washing clothes properly is a grooming practice concerned with cleaning garments so that odour, dirt and stains are removed and fabrics last. In appearance communities it is raised mainly in connection with clothing that retains smell.
Laundry typically involves washing with detergent, agitation, rinsing and drying; Wikipedia notes that warmer water increases chemical activity and stain solubility, while heat and agitation can shrink wool and cold water reduces colour bleeding. The article does not discuss odour specifically.

name: Laundry sanitiser and strip washing

chain: Sanitiser or strip wash on gym kit
angle.text: Gym-goers use laundry sanitisers and heavy strip washes to get persistent odour out of sports clothing. Results are described through popular anecdotes, with no dedicated studies.

summary: Extra washing tricks for smelly gym kit; popular anecdotes, no dedicated studies.
note: Check garment care labels; heat can damage some fabrics.
currentQuick:
Some people use sanitising additives or long soaks to get smell out of workout clothes.
No study found here tests these methods.
How it works: The aim is to kill or wash away odour-producing bacteria and residue; heat and drying are the factors general references mention.
Risks and caveats: Heat and agitation can shrink or damage some fabrics, so care labels apply.[1]
deepLead:
Laundry sanitiser and strip washing are practices discussed for removing persistent odour from gym and sports clothing. Sanitisers are additives intended to kill microorganisms in the wash, while strip washing is a heavy soak and wash intended to remove built-up residue.
No source reviewed here covers either practice in detail. Wikipedia's laundry article says high temperatures kill microorganisms, though it flags the claim as uncited, and says drying at 60 degrees Celsius or higher for thirty minutes kills many mites. Body odour is generally attributed to bacteria acting on skin secretions, which can transfer to fabric.

name: Wool and merino clothes

chain: Merino fabric worn next to skin
angle.text: Users wear merino wool as a fabric said to resist odour, so clothes stay fresh between washes. The claim is popular in appearance and grooming discussions and untested in the sources reviewed.

note: Wool can shrink with heat and agitation.

Merino is a fine, soft wool used for clothing. People interested in smelling clean say it stays fresher than other fabrics.

How it works: Odour arises from bacteria acting on sweat; proponents believe wool limits this, though no reviewed source confirms it.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes heat and agitation shrink wool, and that a 2004 mulesing campaign led some retailers to drop Australian merino.[1][3]
deepLead:
Merino is a fine, soft wool from the Merino sheep breed, used in clothing. In appearance and grooming discussions it is mentioned as a fabric that resists odour.
Wikipedia says the Merino breed originated in the Iberian Peninsula in the High Middle Ages and that its wool is generally under 24 microns in diameter. That article does not address odour resistance, and no study found here compares merino with other fabrics for smell.

name: Cedar shoe inserts

angle.text: Users place cedar shoe trees in footwear between wearings to limit shoe and foot odour and keep shoes in shape. Cedar is commonly said to absorb moisture and add its own scent; no trials on odour exist.

note: No studies on cedar for odour were found.
currentQuick:
Cedar inserts are wooden forms left in shoes between wears. They keep shape and are said to absorb moisture and add a woody scent.
In grooming circles they are used as a passive odour measure alongside sock and hygiene habits.
How it works: Proponents say the porous wood draws moisture out of the shoe. Foot odour itself is attributed to bacteria acting on sweat.
Risks and caveats: No documented harms were found; no studies on odour effects were found either.
deepLead:
Cedar shoe inserts are wooden pieces, often shaped like shoe trees, placed in footwear between wearings. A shoe tree is described generally as a device placed in a shoe to preserve its shape. In appearance and grooming communities they are discussed as a way to limit foot and shoe odour, since cedar is commonly said to absorb moisture and carry its own scent.
Foot odour is generally attributed to sweat combined with bacterial activity, and general references list foot hygiene, sock choice and medicated insoles among prevention measures. No source consulted for this entry examines cedar specifically.

name: Foot powder

angle.text: Users dust foot powder onto feet and into shoes to keep them dry and cut odour as part of a grooming routine. Some formulations add antifungal or deodorant agents; evidence is indirect.

summary: Dusting powder for sweaty feet; sensible and cheap, but evidence is indirect.

currentQuick:
Foot powder is applied to feet or shoes to absorb moisture and reduce odour. Some products add antifungal or deodorant agents.
A 1974 swimming-bath report linked powder sachets to fewer athlete's foot cases, but no trial of cosmetic odour control was found.
How it works: Powders absorb sweat; odour is attributed to bacteria breaking down sweat and dead skin.
Risks and caveats: Contact allergy to an antimicrobial ingredient in one deodorant foot powder has been reported.
deepLead:
Foot powder is a dusting powder applied to the feet and sometimes inside shoes to absorb moisture and reduce odour, and some formulations contain antifungal or deodorant agents. It is used in grooming routines to manage foot sweat and odour.
Evidence is mostly indirect. A 1974 report from a swimming bath found that supplying foot powder sachets to bathers coincided with a fall in tinea pedis incidence, and a skin-product study included a foot powder among four products tested for effects on the skin microbiome. Contact allergy to an antimicrobial ingredient in one deodorant foot powder has been reported.

name: Showering twice daily

angle.text: Appearance-focused users shower morning and evening, or after exercise, to control body odour and keep skin and hair clean. It is a common habit, and the twice-daily frequency itself has not been studied.

deepLead:
Showering twice daily is a hygiene routine, usually morning and evening or after exercise, adopted in appearance-focused communities to control body odour and keep skin and hair clean. Personal hygiene is generally described as cleanliness practices for health and social acceptance, and norms vary by culture and era.
No published trial comparing twice-daily showering with once-daily showering for appearance or odour was found in the sources consulted.

name: Scent layering (body wash, lotion, fragrance)

angle.text: Users stack matching body wash, lotion and fragrance so their scent builds and lasts longer through the day. The fragrance industry promotes versions of the practice; its effect on longevity is untested.

summary: Stacking matched wash, lotion and fragrance to make a scent last; popular, untested.
note: More scented products means more potential allergens.
currentQuick:
Scent layering uses products from the same scent family, such as body wash, lotion and fragrance, so the smell lasts and feels coherent.
The fragrance industry itself suggests layering through the day.
How it works: Moisturised skin is said to hold fragrance longer, and a matching base reinforces the top scent.
Risks and caveats: Fragrance ingredients can be allergenic; no layering-specific studies were found.
deepLead:
Scent layering is the practice of using matching or complementary scented products, such as body wash, lotion and fragrance, in sequence so the smell builds and lasts longer. The fragrance industry promotes a version of it: scented bath oil, shower gel or lotion in the morning, a lighter eau de toilette in the afternoon, and perfume at pulse points in the evening.
No published trials of layering were found. General references say hydrated skin holds fragrance longer and that diet, medications and dry skin can alter how a scent develops.

A signature scent is a single fragrance a person wears consistently so that others come to associate it with them. In appearance communities it is discussed as a memorability and personal-branding tool.
Perfume references cite many long-running fragrances, such as Chanel No. 5 and Guerlain's Shalimar, as classics. Fragrance families include floral, amber, woody, fougere and fresh, and concentration labels (parfum, eau de parfum, eau de toilette) vary in strength between brands. No studies of signature scents and social perception were found.

Hair perfume or hair mist is a light fragrance spray made for the hair, as an alternative to applying perfume to skin. It is used to leave scent in the hair and is discussed in grooming communities as a way to add a scent trail.
Perfume references classify light 'mists' and splashes as low-concentration products (eau fraiche, 3% or less aromatic compounds), and general references note that perfume materials can include allergenic compounds. No studies of hair-specific fragrances were found, and the perfume reference consulted does not address hair products.
